title: Three Ways to Turn a Page

blocks.c: Three Ways to Turn a Page

Every reader holds a quiet, lifelong opinion about how text should move. Some want pages that turn, decisively, the way paper turns. Some want to sink down through a chapter the way you sink through a long letter. Some want the entire book to be one continuous corridor with no doors in it at all. This app declines to referee the question. It offers all three ways and keeps its own opinion to itself.

items: Paged — the text stands still and turns when you say so. The nearest thing to paper, and the kindest to a mind that likes to look up and find the paragraph still where it left it.
Scroll — one chapter at a time, top to bottom, with the next chapter waiting politely behind a bar at the end.
Endless — chapters follow one another without a seam, for readers who would rather not be reminded that chapters end.

blocks.c: Changing between them takes two taps. Tap the page once to call the controls back, then find the small button marked Aa in the header. The sheet that rises holds the reader's settings, and its first row is the mode row — Paged, Scroll, Endless, three plain words. Tap one now, if you are curious. This is the chapter for experiments, and nothing you try in it is permanent.

Notice what did not happen when you switched. You did not lose your place. The paragraph you were reading was re-set, re-flowed, and put back in front of you in the new shape, without being asked. The app treats your position in the text as the one sacred thing it manages. Modes are furniture. The text is the house, and you were not moved out of it.

As for which mode to choose — we can offer observations, not verdicts. Paged suits long, dense books, and any hour when you want the sentence to stand still while you think about it. Scroll suits shorter chapters, and reading with one hand on a crowded train. Endless suits serials, and the particular time of night when stopping is a decision you would rather not be asked to make twenty times.
There is no correct way to move through a book. There is only the way that lets you forget you are moving at all.

And if you close that sheet and never open it again, that is a legitimate choice too. Every default in this app was picked to be livable. The Aa button is not homework. It is a standing offer, and it will still be standing in a year.
It has more to offer than modes, though. The next chapter is about the letters themselves.
